belief: Being poor means being lazy or bad.
origins: This belief is common because it is comforting: if poverty is always someone’s fault, then we are safe from it. It appears in family sayings, political rhetoric, and even misread proverbs. Those who have lived in poverty often absorb it too, and feel shame for a situation shaped by many forces such as illness, lost jobs, family needs, education, and bad luck.
teaches: Proverbs does say that diligence is rewarded, but Scripture also says that whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, and whoever is kind to the needy honors Him. Jesus said, “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.” James asks whether God has not chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith. Jesus said that whatever we did for the least of these, we did for Him. Poverty is not a verdict on character, and the poor are close to God’s heart.
self_statements: If I were not lazy, I would not be poor.
Poor people just need to try harder.
I am to blame for my situation.
People think poor people are bad.
I should be ashamed of needing help.
errors: Blaming character for what is shaped by circumstances.
Believing that people always get what they deserve.
Blaming myself for forces beyond my control.
Treating one group as all alike.
questions: What factors beyond effort shape a person’s finances?
Do I know people who work hard and are still poor? What does that tell me?
Where did I learn that poverty equals laziness?
What does God say about the poor and about those who judge them?
How has this belief affected how I treat others or myself?
What would more compassion look like?
truth: Poverty is often shaped by illness, job loss, family needs, education, and many things beyond a person’s control. God honors the poor and calls us to kindness. I can take responsibility for what is mine to do, without carrying a verdict of laziness or badness.
hw_truths: Poverty is not a verdict on character.
Kindness to the needy honors God.
Effort matters, and so do circumstances.
I can take responsibility without self-blame.
log: Each week, note one time you chose compassion over judgment, for yourself or someone else.
actions: Write the circumstances that shaped your situation or someone you know.
Write a fair description in place of “lazy” or “bad.”
Do one practical act of kindness for someone in need.
Ask God to shape your view of the poor.
prayer: Father, You honor the poor. Forgive me for the times I have judged, and free me from the shame that says poverty means I am bad. Give me compassion for myself and others and wisdom for the steps I can take. Amen.
hw_questions: Where did I learn this belief?
How do I treat people in need?
What does God say about the poor?
What would compassion look like for me?
What is one practical act of kindness?
name_example: Sarah can write: “God honors the poor, so I can leave behind the label of lazy or bad.”
